name: Tomas Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm at Kessler Auto by half seven, it's a six-bay garage off the ring road, and the first job is usually whatever's been dropped off overnight with a warning light on. These days half of what we see is hybrids, so I spend a lot of time with the scan tool and an AI app on my phone that reads the fault codes back to me in plain words and pulls up wiring diagrams. I like the puzzle part best, when a car has an odd fault and you chase it down. What wears me out is the cold in winter and the days when it's all brake pads and oil changes, eight in a row.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who else is in the workshop with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rolf Kessler owns the place, he's in his fifties and still does the welding himself. There are three of us mechanics, plus Hanne on the front desk doing bookings and quotes. I live with my girlfriend Ines, she's a dental nurse, and we rent a flat above a bakery about ten minutes away. We've got maybe three months of bills put aside, which feels okay but not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at the garage: the tools got a bit smarter, that's all. The scan tool explains codes better, the booking system texts people, fine. Cars still need someone to get under them. Online I'd probably post something like, told you so, the hype was overblown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays pretty much how it is, and that's not bad. I'd keep using the AI app for diagnostics because it saves me twenty minutes a car. The real pressure for me isn't AI, it's rent going up and Ines and me wanting to buy somewhere one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the high-voltage course for electric cars that Rolf keeps saying he'll pay half of, because that's where the work is heading anyway. I'd push to take on more of the hybrid jobs since I'm the one who likes them. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month toward a deposit, maybe 200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, to be honest. It's a normal life, and I like normal. Maybe a little bored by the idea, because I was curious to see what the tools would do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ines over dinner that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we can stop joking about the robots coming for my spanners. My real worry isn't robots. The bakery below our flat smells lovely, but our rent went up twice in two years. So we'd end up talking about the deposit again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the garage would you think about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Hanne on the front desk, because the booking and quotes are the bit that's already getting automated, even in a slow world. If the software does reminders and quotes, Rolf might cut her hours. The mechanics would be fine.

say: The tools got **a bit smarter**, but cars still need someone underneath them.
I'd say online that **the hype** was overblown, like I expected.
think: My job stays the same, and the AI app keeps saving me **twenty minutes** a car.
My real pressure is **rent** and saving for a place with Ines, not AI.
do: Finish the **high-voltage course** for electric cars, with Rolf paying half.
Take on more of the **hybrid jobs** that most of the others avoid.
Put **200 a month** aside toward a deposit on a flat.
feel: Relaxed and settled, with a little **boredom** because he was curious about what came next.
S0.quote: My real worry isn't robots. The bakery below our flat smells lovely, but our rent went up twice in two years.
fieldNote: He **already uses AI** daily and talks about it like any other workshop tool.
His worries in this world are **housing costs**, not his work.
He noticed the front-desk job is the **soft spot**, even in a slow world.

steps.text: Keep fixing cars at Kessler Auto using the AI diagnostic app
Finish the high-voltage electric car course this year
Put 200 a month toward a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our chance, honestly. If the software does quotes, parts ordering and the first look at fault codes, we get more time with our hands on the car. Online I'd say mechanics should learn the tools now instead of moaning about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the part of my job that made me feel clever is the diagnosis, and that's exactly what AI gets good at. If any apprentice with a tablet can find the fault, my edge shrinks and so might my pay rise. My hands are safe for now, but the brains part of the job gets cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask Rolf to make me the person who runs the new diagnostic and booking system, so I'm the one who knows it inside out. I'd finish the high-voltage course and look at a short course on driver-assist cameras and sensors, because calibrating those is fiddly hands-on work. I'd keep the 200 a month going into savings and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit restless, I think. I'm not scared for myself yet, but I can see the ground moving under the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Hanne on the front desk in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hanne's job is the first to go, I'm pretty sure. Customers would book through an app and get an AI quote before they even ring. I'd feel bad, because Hanne (the garage receptionist) is the one who remembers every customer's dog's name, and software won't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said this is a chance, but also that your edge shrinks. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. It's a chance if I move first and a problem if I sit still. If the fault-finding gets cheap, the guy who knows how to set up the cameras on a new car and fix the stuff the software can't reach is still worth paying.

say: This is **our chance** to spend more time with our hands on the car.
Mechanics should **learn the tools** now instead of moaning about them.
think: Diagnosis is the part that made him feel clever, and **AI gets good** at it.
If anyone with a tablet finds faults, his **pay rise** could shrink.
do: Ask Rolf to make him the **go-to person** for the new diagnostic and booking system.
Take a short course on **calibrating cameras** and sensors on newer cars.
Keep the **200 a month** going into savings without touching it.
feel: **Restless** rather than scared, watching the ground move under people around him.
S1.quote: The part of my job that made me feel clever is the diagnosis, and that's exactly what AI gets good at.
fieldNote: He sees his **thinking work** shrinking before his hands-on work does.
He holds two views at once: **chance and threat**, depending on whether he moves first.
He worries more for **Hanne** on the front desk than for himself.

steps.text: Run the garage's new AI diagnostic and booking system for Rolf
Take a short course on calibrating driver-assist cameras and sensors
Keep 200 a month going into savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say, well, at least cars still need hands for a few years. I'd probably joke at the garage that we've got until 2031 before the robot takes my creeper board. Online I'd say governments were asleep and should have seen it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the thinking side of my job is gone in 2028, so the garage only needs fewer, cheaper hands. Then by 2031 it doesn't need my hands either. I'd be 32 with three years of rent saved at best, and no trade. That's the part that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in mechatronics, that's robots and electronics together, this winter, because somebody has to fix the robots. I'd stop the flat deposit and keep that money as a cushion, and cut the gym and the car payments, maybe sell my car and ride a bike. Once AGI lands, I'd look for work at whatever firm services the first workshop robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, honestly. I'm usually the one who's excited about new stuff, and here I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we put the flat on hold, not forever, just until we know where my work lands. She'd be fine with it, a dental nurse is hands-on with people, so she's probably safer than me. I'd hate being the one who held us back, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not much warning. What changes because of that short time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't finish a proper qualification before the diagnosis work goes. The robots arriving three years later is the only reason I'd have a shot. I'd be learning robotics while my hours drop, and so would every other mechanic in town.

say: Cars still need **hands** for a few years, so we've got until 2031.
**Governments** were asleep and should have seen this coming.
think: The **thinking side** goes in 2028 and the garage needs fewer, cheaper hands.
By 2031 he could be **32 with no trade** and a few months saved.
do: Start a part-time **mechatronics course** this winter to learn to fix robots.
Pause the **flat deposit** and sell his car to keep a bigger cushion.
Look for work at firms that **service workshop robots** once AGI lands.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, and unsettled that new tech doesn't excite him this time.
S2.quote: With two years I can't finish a proper qualification before the diagnosis work goes. The robots arriving three years later is the only reason I'd have a shot.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** is his whole plan; without it he has none.
He expects **fewer hours** soon and his job to go by 2031.
He worries about **holding Ines back** more than about his own pride.

steps.text: Start a part-time mechatronics course this winter
Sell his car and cancel the gym to stretch savings
Apply to firms that service workshop robots after 2028
Put the flat purchase with Ines on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, we've got a few years, let's use them. At the garage I'd tell the younger lads to start learning electronics now. Online I'd probably share courses and things that actually help mechanics, not doom posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to change direction without a crash. I've got about eight years of hands-on work left. The diagnosis side goes around 2031 and the spanner side around 2034, and that's a real runway if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the mechatronics course over two years at evening classes, while working full time at Kessler Auto. I'd ask Rolf whether he'd go halves on it, since he'll want someone who can look after any robot he buys. We'd probably still buy a small flat with Ines, but a cheaper one, so the mortgage is something one wage can carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can work with. It feels like a long drive with a clear map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, mostly. We'd skip the big trip next summer and put that money into the course and savings. I'd keep my car, because I need it for the evening classes across town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one wage should carry the mortgage. Why one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can't promise mine will be there in 2034. Ines is the steadier earner in that world. If I'm between jobs for a year while I switch, I don't want us losing the flat.

say: We've got **a few years**, so let's use them properly.
He'd share **useful courses** online instead of doom posts.
think: Five years gives him about **eight years** of hands-on work left.
That's a **real runway** to change direction if he doesn't waste it.
do: Study **mechatronics** at evening classes over two years while working full time.
Ask Rolf to **split the course fees** in return for robot upkeep later.
Buy a **cheaper flat** whose mortgage one wage can carry.
feel: **Uneasy** but workable, like a long drive with a clear map.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to change direction without a crash. I've got about eight years of hands-on work left.
fieldNote: He turns the warning time into a **concrete timetable**, counting the robot gap.
He plans the household around **one wage**, quietly expecting a gap in his own.
More **settled** here than in the fast picture, though the end point is the same.

steps.text: Take evening mechatronics classes over two years
Skip next summer's holiday to pay for the course
Buy a cheaper flat with Ines that one wage covers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a whole career change, so nobody should panic. At the garage I'd say the smart move is to be the guy who installs and fixes the robots. Online I'd tell people to pick a skill near the machines and start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really think ten years suits someone my age. I'd be 37 when the thinking side goes and about 40 when the robots arrive. I could finish a proper qualification, get a few years in, and be useful when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Kessler Auto and do a two-year robotics technician course starting in about three years, once it's clearer which machines win. Meanwhile I'd use every AI tool I can at work so I'm good with them. Ines and I would buy the flat in the next couple of years and maybe think about kids around 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, a bit unsettled when I picture being 40 and starting again. But I've always liked new tools, so part of me is curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait three years before the course. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because right now nobody knows which robots will end up in garages. If I train on the wrong system I've wasted two years. I'd rather watch for a bit while I keep learning the AI tools, then jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for kids you might have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to be good with their hands and with machines, both. If I end up fixing the robots that replaced me, I'd want my kids to understand that's not a defeat. It's just the next tool.

say: Ten years is **a whole career change**, so nobody should panic.
The smart move is to **install and fix** the robots.
think: At 37 the thinking side goes, and robots arrive around **age 40**.
There's time to finish a **proper qualification** and get experience first.
do: Use **every AI tool** at work for the next few years to stay sharp.
Start a two-year **robotics technician course** in about three years.
Buy the **flat with Ines** in the next couple of years.
feel: Mostly okay and **curious**, with some unease about starting again at 40.
S4.quote: If I end up fixing the robots that replaced me, I'd want my kids to understand that's not a defeat.
fieldNote: He'd **wait and watch** before picking a robotics course, to avoid the wrong system.
Ten years lets him keep **family plans** like a flat and children.
His **curiosity** about tools softens a fear he still names.

steps.text: Use the AI diagnostic and quoting tools on every job
Start a two-year robotics technician course around 2029
Buy a flat with Ines within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. Not because the end is different, but because I'd be learning robots while my hours are already shrinking, and so would everyone else. What would help is cheap evening courses for mechanics and someone, the government or the garages, paying people a bit while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who ends up owning the robots. If it's big chains, small garages like Kessler Auto die. If small garages can lease the robots, the local garage might survive, and that matters for where people like me end up.

headlineQuote: If small garages can lease the robots, the local garage might survive, and that matters for where people like me end up.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old mechanic** at a six-bay garage who likes chasing odd hybrid faults.
He uses an **AI diagnostic app** daily and sees new tools as part of the trade.
His steady worry is **rent**, and saving with his girlfriend Ines for a flat.
In the AGI pictures he plans to **retrain in mechatronics** and fix the robots himself.
The **two-year warning** shakes him most, because it gives him no runway.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be retraining while his hours shrink and everyone competes.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap evening courses** for mechanics, with some pay while they retrain.
Ways for **small garages** to lease robots so the local trade survives.
